lha-7.nm: Office of the Chief of Naval Operations
lha-7.tx:
SAILORS FIRST SUNDAY: Sailor Of The Week ⚓

Congratulations to HM2 Brandon W. Williams, a Colorado native who serves as the SAR Medical Technician Standardization Leading Petty Officer (LPO) with Helicopter Sea Combat Squadron Two-Five (HSC-25) in Agana, Guam!

As medical department LPO, he led five HMs and advised one Senior Medical Officer in FDNF command medical readiness, pre/post deployment medical requirements, and medical training for 435 sailors from HSC-25, AIMD, ASD, AIMD Bahrain, VUP-19, and ERCS Naval Hospital Guam. 

His leadership resulted in treating 560 patients, inoculating 125 service members from Influenza, Japanese Encephalitis and Hepatitis, 18 flight physicals, 109 post-deployment health assessments and 53 pre-deployment health screenings, contributing to 92% squadron medical readiness, as well as the deployment of Detachment 3 and Detachment 6 in support of ESB-6/ LHA-7.

As a Search and Rescue Medical Technician, Williams responded directly to two Medevacs, including one stroke patient that required urgent intervention to prevent neurological deterioration and one renal failure patient that required higher-level care, impacting two souls saved. As Command Tactical Combat Casualty Care Program Director, his instruction has qualified 73 personnel in TCCC tier 2, as well as 19 enlisted in TCCC All Service Member. 

His professionalism, leadership, and unwavering commitment exemplify the standards expected of our Navy’s finest Sailors!

qt.t:
Per @Liz_Friden The U.S. is sending the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group and the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit to the Middle East, two U.S. officials confirm to Fox News. The ships will arrive in the Middle East by the end of November, the officials said. These new deployments will add about 10,000 Sailors and Marines to the Middle East.

The USS Roosevelt will be the third aircraft carrier in the Middle East, joining the USS George H.W. Bush which arrived to the region in April, and the USS George Washington which arrived in mid-August to replace the USS Abraham Lincoln. This will provide more options for the U.S. as President Trump is reportedly considering ramping up strikes on Iran after the Midterms. 

The USS Roosevelt departed its home port of San Diego on Sunday and the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit deployed from San Diego on Monday along with the Makin Island Amphibious Ready Group. The Marine Expeditionary Unit and Amphibious Ready Group typically include about 4,200 Marines and Sailors. The USS Roosevelt carrier strike group includes about 6,000 Sailors.

The ships will arrive in the Middle East by the end of November, the officials said. These new deployments will add about 10,000 Sailors and Marines to the Middle East.

The USS Roosevelt will be the third aircraft carrier in the Middle East, joining the USS George H.W. Bush which arrived to the region in April, and the USS George Washington which arrived in mid-August to replace the USS Abraham Lincoln. The USS Roosevelt departed its home port of San Diego on Sunday and the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit deployed from San Diego on Monday along with the Makin Island Amphibious Ready Group. Correction: H/T @Liz_Friden and @JM_Szuba

The TR and the Makin left San Diego on Sept 27 and Sept 28 respectively, meaning the U.S. is still on track to have three aircraft carriers in the Middle East in November. While the USS Roosevelt is capable of getting to the Middle East by the end of next week, one senior U.S. official Fox spoke with said the carrier will likely arrive by the end of November.

The USS George H.W. Bush carrier strike group and the USS George Washington carrier strike group are both currently in the Arabian Sea.

BIG | 🇺🇸🇮🇷🇮🇱‼️‼️ The United States is reportedly preparing a major expansion of its military presence near Iran, with a third aircraft carrier strike group and thousands of additional personnel expected to deploy to the Middle East.

According to reports attributed to Fox News, Washington is sending the USS Theodore Roosevelt Carrier Strike Group and the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit to the region, potentially adding approximately 10,000 sailors and Marines by late November. The Theodore Roosevelt would reportedly join the USS George H.W. Bush and USS George Washington carrier strike groups near Iran, bringing the total to three. The buildup comes amid claims that President Donald Trump is considering expanded military strikes against Iran following the November midterm elections. The precise deployment arrangements and reported plans for further strikes remain unconfirmed.

The concentration of three American carrier strike groups would represent a substantial increase in US naval aviation and strike capabilities around Iran. Combined with additional Marine forces, the deployment could strengthen Washington’s ability to conduct sustained military operations, defend regional partners, and respond to Iranian retaliation. However, a larger military presence does not by itself establish that a decision to launch new strikes has been made.

lhd-4.t: If you want to understand what it means to be an American citizen, look at what happened in the Indian Ocean on Easter Sunday, April 12, 2009. One merchant cap…
lhd-4.tx:
If you want to understand what it means to be an American citizen, look at what happened in the Indian Ocean on Easter Sunday, April 12, 2009.

One merchant captain from Vermont named Richard Phillips was being held hostage inside a covered orange lifeboat by Somali pirates armed with AK-47s.

He was not a general. He was not a politician. He was one cargo ship captain who had offered himself as a hostage to save his crew.

To bring that one man home, the United States sent the guided-missile destroyer USS Bainbridge, the frigate USS Halyburton, the amphibious assault ship USS Boxer, and a team of U.S. Navy SEALs who parachuted straight into the black ocean at night.

For four days, the lifeboat pitched violently in rough seas twenty-five yards behind the destroyer.

Then at dusk on Sunday, a pirate pressed the barrel of his AK-47 directly against Captain Phillips' back and prepared to kill him.

On the fantail of the USS Bainbridge, three Navy SEAL snipers lay braced in the dark. The destroyer was rolling in one direction. The tiny lifeboat was pitching in another. If even one sniper missed by half an inch, or fired a tenth of a second late, the hostage would die.

Through night-vision scopes, all three snipers waited for the exact millisecond when three targets appeared in the tiny windows at once.

One word came over the headset.

Three rifles fired as a single sound.

All three kidnappers dropped instantly. Captain Phillips walked onto the deck of the USS Bainbridge without a scratch.

Do not touch a citizen of a country that will drop Navy SEALs from the sky at midnight for one man.

qt.t:
🇺🇸 U.S. Navy has doubled its fleet capacity to operate the MQ-25A Stingray unmanned aircraft system (UAS) over a five-month period, standing up a second operational MD-5C Ground Control Station (GCS). @USNavy 

MD-5C, powered by Lockheed Martin Skunk Works MDCX autonomy platform, is installed in the Unmanned Air Warfare Center (UAWC), the dedicated shipboard command center for unmanned carrier aviation. The Navy's Nimitz-class aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt (CVN 71) received the first operational MD-5C in March 2026, followed by her sister ship USS Ronald Reagan (CVN 76) in August 2026. @LockheedMartin 

The MD-5C is a highly complex system-of-systems, which includes the government Command, Control, Communications, Computers and Intelligence (C4I) network, MDCX software and hardware, and additional government-produced ancillary equipment. Within the GCS, MDCX is the mission planning and execution software that enables Navy operators to command and control the MQ-25A Stingray, extending carrier air wing reach and freeing manned aircraft for higher-priority missions.

#USNavy #MQ25A #MD5C #MDCX #LockheedMartin #SkunkWorks

cvn-76.tx:
🇺🇸 Boeing, U.S. Navy and Lockheed Martin MQ-25 Integrated Test Team (ITT) established a beyond-line-of-sight (BLOS) satellite command-and-control (C2) link between the MQ-25A Stingray uncrewed aerial fefueler and a production MD-5C control station aboard aircraft carrier USS Ronald Reagan while the ship operated at port and at sea. @BoeingDefense @USNavy @LockheedMartin 

This marked the first time the aircraft was controlled from a carrier using the ground control station and Navy communications network used in operational missions.

The test validated an end-to-end BLOS C2 capability over the Navy’s operational command, control, communications, computers, and intelligence (C4I) network enabling shipboard teams can reliably monitor and command the MQ-25A from an aircraft carrier.

This demonstration is one in a series of buildup exercises designed to validate procedures, networks and interfaces ahead of a risk reduction flight-test program that will include carrier at-sea operations.

#USNavy #Boeing #MQ25A #MD5C

cvn-76.t: The USS Ronald Reagan remotely controlled a Boeing MQ-25A Stingray tanker drone over more than 2,100 statute miles (3,379 km), the U.S. Navy said on 19 October…
cvn-76.tx:
The USS Ronald Reagan remotely controlled a Boeing MQ-25A Stingray tanker drone over more than 2,100 statute miles (3,379 km), the U.S. Navy said on 19 October.

The carrier in the Pacific linked to the aircraft at Boeing’s facility in Mascoutah, Illinois, via an MD-5C ground station and a low-Earth-orbit satellite network. It is a beyond-line-of-sight command test, not a refuelling flight. The Reagan’s Unmanned Air Warfare Center was installed after 11 ship modifications. The Theodore Roosevelt got the first operational MD-5C in March.

The Stingray is 15.54 metres (51 feet) long with a 22.86-metre (75-foot) span. It is meant to offload 6,350 kilograms (14,000 pounds) of fuel at 926 kilometres (500 nautical miles). The programme covers 76 aircraft, including 67 operational tankers, at about $19.4 billion, with initial operational capability planned for 2029. 

It is intended to free Super Hornets from tanker duty.

#USNavy #MQ25A #Stingray #Boeing #USSRonaldReagan #DroneWars

🚨Labour presses on with Chagos handover despite Trump’s opposition

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has confirmed negotiations will continue to transfer sovereignty of the Chagos Islands to Mauritius while leasing back the joint US-UK base on Diego Garcia. After reviewing the issue “with a fresh pair of eyes”, he concluded a deal is still necessary to avoid legal uncertainty over the strategically vital facility.
The arrangement is set to cost £165 million a year for the first three years, then £120 million annually for the remaining 96 years. Critics put the long-term bill far higher. 🇮🇷|New Missiles Launched in Central Iran

October 24, 2026. Central Iran. Footage of a missile test has emerged. Based on the ballistic trajectory, this appears to be a new type of ballistic missile system undergoing operational testing.

💥 This is not merely a "test launch," it is an "acceptance test prior to delivery."

As IRGC spokesperson Mohebbi previously stated, Iran’s missile stockpile has increased by 150%, with significant improvements in quality including greater range, higher precision, and enhanced destructive power. "Should the war escalate, surprises will be revealed."

These tests represent the first installment of those "surprises."

🎯 The Timing of the Tests

Russia has just confirmed that its personnel have not been evacuated from the Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant. Russian nuclear experts and diplomats remain on-site, signaling to Washington and Tel Aviv: you may issue threats, but those threats will not force our withdrawal.

On the same day, Iran conducts tests of a new missile system. This is no coincidence; it is a dual-track signal, Russia’s deterrent presence at Bushehr, combined with Iran’s missile capabilities in its interior.

📜 What Is This System?

Based on its ballistic profile, this appears to be a two-stage, solid-fuel system equipped with a maneuverable re-entry vehicle (MaRV). Solid-fuel propulsion eliminates the need for on-site fueling or lengthy preparation, allowing for launch within minutes of leaving storage. The MaRV capability enables the warhead to alter its trajectory during the terminal phase, effectively thwarting the predictive calculations of interceptor systems.

This is not just an increase in quantity; it is a qualitative leap. The system’s range covers Israel, U.S. military bases in Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait, the UAE, and Saudi Arabia, as well as the U.S. facility on Diego Garcia in the Indian Ocean.

⚔️ The Location of the Tests

The tests took place in Central Iran not near the borders or the coast, but deep within the country’s interior. This means the launch sites are situated far from the Strait of Hormuz and the Persian Gulf coastline, protected by layers of air defense systems and positioned well beyond the operational radius of U.S. carrier strike groups.

A missile launched from the interior is far more difficult to destroy in a preemptive strike than one launched from the coast. 

🔻 The Ledger

The United States has spent $11 billion on missile defense for Israel, firing 609 interceptors. Now, Iran is testing new systems.

This is not an "arms race." It is "cost imposition." The cost of a single interceptor is dozens of times higher than that of an offensive missile. Every time the U.S. intercepts one, it loses money. Every time Iran tests a new system, it drives up the cost of U.S. interception.

A nation that can still test new missile systems in the eighth month of a war is not collapsing. It is declaring: My production lines are running. My engineers are innovating. My missiles are taking flight.

Long live Iran. Long live the Resistance. Long live the Axis of Resistance.

incirlik.t: Trump openly lies that Zelenskyy “doesn’t care” about ending the war. He also lies that Russia is generously sending cheap diesel to the world. Russia is selli…
incirlik.tx:
Trump openly lies that Zelenskyy “doesn’t care” about ending the war. He also lies that Russia is generously sending cheap diesel to the world. Russia is selling it under a deal Trump struck with Putin, after the US lifted sanctions to allow it.

Russia invaded Ukraine. Russia can stop the war any day by withdrawing. Ukraine can’t. 

Breakdown of Trump lies⬇️

“I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table.”

Trump lied.

Trump’s own words give other reasons for going easy on Russia. Later in the same post he says that perhaps more importantly, Russia is doing very little to help Iran and he wants to keep it that way. Bloomberg reported that he waived the Russia energy tariffs because they were getting in the way of lowering diesel prices before the midterms. When he announced the diesel deal with Putin, he didn’t mention the war or sanctions and performatively called lower prices for farmers, ranchers and truckers his greatest priority, all the meanwhile being the culprit behind the increased prices.

He has shown no similar concern about driving Ukraine away. He said Kyiv "had better damn well stop" its refinery strikes and that Ukraine should replace its president, and Ukrainian officials say US counterparts warned that the US would cut off intelligence if the strikes continued. Russia, meanwhile, hit power plants in Ukraine within hours of Trump announcing his energy ceasefire.

"Russia is doing very little, if anything, to help the Islamic Republic of Iran.”

Trump lied.

“Very little compared to what they could be doing” is a standard nobody can test. Moscow and Tehran have a deep military relationship. Russia’s air war on Ukrainian cities was built on Iranian-designed Shahed drones.

Read the sentence in context. Trump says he wants to keep Russia’s help to Iran limited and will, unless stupid people get in the way. That’s an admission that he’s going easy on Moscow over Ukraine to keep it quiet on Iran.

His own military has said otherwise. Gen. Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, confirmed Russia has been aiding Iran during the war, including expanded intelligence sharing and satellite imagery to help Tehran target US forces. Ukraine has said Russian satellites photographed Diego Garcia, Incirlik in Turkey, Al Udeid in Qatar and Saudi oil and gas fields, all of which Iran later attacked.

Russia was shipping TNT, ammunition and drone components to Iran across the Caspian Sea, helping it rebuild arsenals used up fighting the US and Israel. Moscow has also coached Tehran on drone use and electronic warfare, drawing on its experience in Ukraine. Eighteen American service members have been killed in the war. Trump knew this months prior, did nothing to protect service members.

“Farmers, ranchers, and businesses of all kinds are suffering greatly from this.”

Trump lied.

Ukrainian strikes forced Russia to ban diesel exports, which tightened global supply, but the main cause of record US diesel prices is the war with Iran. Tehran closed the Strait of Hormuz after the first US and Israeli strikes in February, and shipping crude out of the Gulf now costs about $33 a barrel, up from about $2. NBC reported that Trump has tried to blame the Ukraine conflict for record diesel prices rather than his own war on Iran.

“Russia is, nevertheless, sending, at a low price, millions of barrels of diesel to the World.”

Trump lied.

Russia isn’t sending diesel out of goodwill. It is selling it under a deal Trump negotiated with Putin, after the Treasury licensed transactions in Russian diesel, including US imports, through April 2027. Russian industry experts had already been calling for the export ban to be lifted because Russia was losing profit. The shipments come to about ten days of US consumption and are expected to do little for prices. Trump provides nothing to back up “at a low price.”

#Tehran has issued a pointed warning to Berlin, declaring that #German military bases and associated facilities throughout the #MiddleEast would be treated as legitimate targets should Germany openly participate in any military operation against Iran, according to a report from the #IRGC-linked Fars News Agency.
The message, conveyed amid rising regional tensions, follows what Iranian sources describe as an escalation of “anti-Iranian measures” by Germany. It also includes demands that Berlin end what Tehran calls the harassment of Iranian residents in Germany based on what it terms baseless accusations—a reference tied to recent German legal actions against individuals linked to Iranian intelligence.
#Iranian officials and media have simultaneously signaled that a new round of direct conflict is viewed as increasingly probable. In the weeks leading up to the warning, Iran has carried out multiple ballistic missile tests, which observers interpret as part of broader preparations and efforts to demonstrate remaining strike capabilities despite earlier damage to its arsenal and production infrastructure.
Potential targets highlighted in the warning focus on German-linked military infrastructure in the wider region. While Germany maintains a comparatively limited permanent footprint in the Middle East relative to the United States or #UnitedKingdom, the statement broadly covers any barracks, bases, or facilities associated with German forces or operations. Related reporting in recent weeks has also drawn attention to concerns over U.S. installations on German soil (such as Ramstein and Spangdahlem), which serve as major logistics and command hubs supporting regional missions, though the Fars warning specifically addresses German assets across the region rather than on German territory itself.
This development occurs against a backdrop of ongoing friction, including German diplomatic summons of Iranian representatives and judicial outcomes involving alleged plots, as Tehran positions itself for possible renewed hostilities.

qt.t:
Big week of @TheUFL meetings on both the business and football operations sides as we prepare for 2027.

As promised, the UFL will be TRANSPARENT. On AND off the field!!!!

Today, our team presented stadium availability for all eight UFL teams. Seven venues offered significant flexibility. Unfortunately, St. Louis was the exception.

Based on the BattleDome dates currently available, the @BattlehawksUFL would play FOUR straight home games, followed by FIVE consecutive road games, and potentially return home for Week 10.

FOUR HOME GAMES. FIVE ROAD GAMES.

Sorry, but that just DOESN’T WORK FOR US!!!!

This isn’t your old spring football league. We’re going to do things DIFFERENTLY!!!! That means better planning, better partnerships, more marketing, more transparency, and most importantly, putting our FANS FIRST!!!!

St. Louis has one of the most passionate fan bases in football. These fans arrive early, stay late, and travel to support their team. I experienced it firsthand at the BattleDome and watching Battlehawks fans travel to Louisville.

I promised St. Louis we would do more, starting with bringing the UFL Draft to St. Louis on November 18.

But promises mean nothing without a

fort-hood.tx:
@RepoleStable Appreciate the transparency and the invitation for ideas. Here’s a practical way to keep the Battlehawks at the Dome while fixing the 4-home / 5-road stretch and doing right by St. Louis fans:

Finish training camp in Arlington, then base the Battlehawks in St. Louis for the first five weeks of the season. Secure short-term player and staff housing so the team is fully embedded in the market. Front-load their first four home games at the BattleDome during that window, then play their fifth “home” game at Fort Leonard Wood as a Hats Off to Heroes military appreciation game for the troops! similar to the historic Fort Hood game the league hosted last year. Fort Leonard Wood is only a couple hours from St. Louis, so it still functions as a regional home date while giving the team a meaningful way to honor service members.

During the five-week residency, lean into local presence: open practices, community events, youth clinics, season-ticket member dinners, and player appearances. Use the stretch as a concentrated marketing push to drive early ticket sales and re-energize the market. Film a short documentary series following the team’s time in St. Louis and the Fort Leonard Wood game, great content that highlights both the fan base and the league’s military outreach.

After the five weeks, return to the hub. Slot one game around Week 7 or 8 in Dallas so the remaining road stretch isn’t five straight. Other teams travel weekly anyway, so the early clustered homes still give St. Louis a strong start (they’ve already had an extra home game in recent years). The temporary residency and military game more than offset the schedule compression by creating real local access, energy, and goodwill.

This also works as a low-risk pilot. The hub model saves money, but it limits true market presence and season-ticket engagement. Testing a short “home residency” with one team, plus a regional military date, could inform how the league handles future scheduling or market development without abandoning the centralized model.

St. Louis fans have shown they’ll show up and travel. Giving them a concentrated, high-visibility home stretch, plus a special game for the troops nearby, turns a tough schedule constrain into something that feels intentional and fan-focused. Worth exploring.

pearl-harbor.t: Three days after Pearl Harbor, someone took a saw to the cherry trees in Washington. Four trees came down. One stump had an angry message carved into it. Lette…
pearl-harbor.tx:
Three days after Pearl Harbor, someone took a saw to the cherry trees in Washington.

Four trees came down. One stump had an angry message carved into it.

Letters poured in demanding the rest be torn out by the roots.

Those trees were a gift from Tokyo. America was now at war with Tokyo.

So Washington made a quiet decision.

They gave the trees a new name. "Oriental" cherry trees.

Not to erase them. To protect them.

It worked. The trees made it through the war.

Then, in 1952, Tokyo had a problem. The riverbank where those trees were born, along the Arakawa River, had withered away during the war.

Tokyo asked America for help.

America sent cuttings from the Washington trees. Back home. To the exact riverbank they came from.

And again in 1981.

Today, that riverbank is lined with cherry trees for nearly three miles. Every April, Tokyo families spread their picnic blankets under them.

My father has gone every spring for 40 years.

Last night I told him where his trees came from.

He was quiet for a while. Then he said, "So they were holding them for us."

America, you could have cut them all down.

You kept them safe instead.

Then you sent them home.

pearl-harbor.t: U.S. Army Private First Class Barney Fushimi Hajiro of Hawaii, was awarded the Medal of Honor for his extraordinary actions on October 19, 1944, near Bruyères…
pearl-harbor.tx:
U.S. Army Private First Class Barney Fushimi Hajiro of Hawaii, was awarded the Medal of Honor for his extraordinary actions on October 19, 1944, near Bruyères and Biffontaine in eastern France.

Hajiro was drafted into the Army two months after the attack on Pearl Harbor. He performed menial labor as part of an engineering battalion until he volunteered to be part of the Army’s all-Nisei 442nd Regimental Combat Team. The 442nd was mostly made up of second-generation American citizens of Japanese descent from Hawaii and the mainland. The unit was sent to Europe and, in May 1944, fought the Germans in Italy, north of Rome. From there, the 442nd was redeployed to France.

On October 19, 1944, the 442nd was fighting near Bruyères and Biffontaine in eastern France and over the next ten days, Hajiro, a private in Company I, repeatedly distinguished himself in battle. He exposed himself to enemy fire while assisting an Allied attack on October 19, and three days later, he and a comrade ambushed an 18-man enemy patrol. On October 29, during the rescue of the so-called "Lost Battalion", which had been surrounded by German forces in the Vosges Mountains, he single-handedly destroyed two German machine gun emplacements. Afterward, he was shot in the shoulder and wrist in another firefight, leaving his left arm partially paralyzed. He was able to rejoin the 442nd in Monte Carlo but was barred from further combat duty. He was then sent back to the United States to recover.

He was awarded the Medal of Honor for his action on October 19, 1944. Hajiro initially received a Distinguished Service Cross but was upgraded to the Medal in 2000 after a 1990s review of U.S. military service records. He was the oldest living Medal of Honor recipient for seven months until he died in January 2011 in Waipahu, Hawaii.

#WeRememberThem

My American brothers and sisters, I have a question for you!

The other day, I saw someone post that Americans don’t use the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki to make fun of Japanese people.

I know we have a complicated history, but personally, I just want Japan and America to keep getting along!

I’m curious to hear what you guys think! 

Sorry if this is a weird question!

qt.t: JUST IN: U.S. military bans Chinese-made BYD vehicles from Kadena Air Base in Okinawa, citing "unacceptable security risks."

kadena.tx:
U.S. Forces Japan(USFJ) just banned every Chinese-made BYD vehicle from Kadena Air Base, the largest U.S. air base overseas.

Starting Monday, October 26, the ban applies at all gates with zero exceptions. Personnel cars, contractor vehicles, taxis, and delivery trucks are all barred.

Base spokesperson Lt. Col. Alli Stormer said the vehicles present “an unacceptable and unmitigable risk to our personnel and our mission.” Officials cite the cameras, sensors, and real-time cloud links in modern connected EVs, which can map surroundings and transmit data from inside a sensitive installation.

Kadena hosts key Pacific air operations and the Typhon system (Tomahawk missiles that can reach Beijing). The move follows the Pentagon’s June 2026 addition of BYD to its Section 1260H list of Chinese military companies, alongside Alibaba, Baidu, and NIO.

Other bases are watching. When everyday cars become potential collection platforms, military sites are forced to treat them as security risks.

nevatim.t: Why is Israel afraid of Egypt, even though Egypt may not have the most advanced weapons, or weapons on par with those of Saudi Arabia and the UAE, for example?…

qt.t:
Egypt’s Air Force looks terrifying on paper.

Until you look under the hood.

Egypt operates roughly 220 F-16s, 54 Rafales and 45 MiG-29M/M2s across these three major fighter fleets. Egypt ordered 54 Rafales in total, with 46 already delivered. More than 300 fighters is a serious force.

But fighter numbers can be deeply misleading.

The biggest weakness is Egypt’s BVR picture.

Its large F-16 fleet does not have AIM-120 AMRAAM, while its MiG-29Ms use R-77 and R-27 missiles. Egypt’s Rafales are its strongest BVR fighters, particularly with Meteor.

But Israel operates in a completely different air combat ecosystem.

The Israeli Air Force combines F-35I stealth fighters, F-15Is and F-16I Sufas, backed by advanced electronic warfare, airborne early warning, intelligence, data link networking, precision weapons and highly integrated command and control.

And then there is the strike side.

Israel has a powerful stand off strike arsenal, including, Golden Horizon, ROCKS, Rampage, LORA and the air launched LORA, designed to hit high value targets such as airbases, air defense systems, command posts and other military infrastructure from stand off distances.

That gives Israel another ma

nevatim.tx:
Why is Israel afraid of Egypt, even though Egypt may not have the most advanced weapons, or weapons on par with those of Saudi Arabia and the UAE, for example?

This is not a call for war. It is an account of the facts and an explanation of how catastrophic a similar war would be for both sides. Here, I will focus on the Israeli side of the equation and explain why such a war would be a disastrous choice for Israel. Quite the opposite, this is a call for peace.

Israel would find it difficult to contemplate going to war with Egypt for the following reasons:

1. Geography

Israel has clear geographical disadvantages, unlike Egypt, which enjoys significant geographical advantages. Israel lacks strategic depth; it is a very small country. The distance from Jerusalem to Tel Aviv is only around 65 km, meaning less than an hour by car. Egypt, by contrast, is a vast country with an area of one million square kilometers. Egypt can absorb the shock of a major war on its territory; Israel cannot do so to the same extent.

2. Egypt could disrupt Israel's military capabilities

Israel's military power relies heavily on its air force and nuclear arsenal. Its air force operates from nine air bases, many of which are located less than 50 km from the Egyptian border, including Hatzor, Nevatim, Ramon, and Ovda. Even the farthest, Ramat David, is only about 270 km away.

This proximity means Egypt could potentially target these bases from relatively safe distances using a combination of air-, sea-, and land-launched munitions, disrupting runways, base infrastructure, and refueling capabilities at the very least, with potentially more serious consequences over time. Some of these bases could even be within artillery range from positions across the border.

3. Egypt could target critical Israeli economic infrastructure

Using the types of munitions in its arsenal, Egypt could potentially target critical economic infrastructure, including seaports, airports, oil refineries, gas fields, and power plants. Precision strikes against these facilities could severely disrupt Israel's economy.

4. The Egyptian navy could impose a Naval blockade on Israel

Egypt possesses a powerful navy that could potentially impose a naval blockade, with Egyptian submarines playing a role in carrying it out.

5. The cost of establishing air superiority over Egypt would be enormous

Egypt is neither Iran nor Syria. It possesses a complex, diverse, and multilayered air defense network, managed by an advanced command-and-control system. Neutralizing a network of this kind would require a major effort, potentially on the scale of what only the world's great military powers could undertake, and at a substantial economic and military cost.

6. The geography of Sinai gives Egypt a defensive advantage

Sinai's passes and narrow corridors constrain an advancing enemy to specific, relatively restricted routes. This gives a well-entrenched defender a significant advantage in stopping an enemy's advance.

qt.t: OBAMA: Iran didn't have nuclear weapons because I had put a deal in place and I didn't have to fire a missile to do it. I just had to engage in diplomacy.

fordow.tx:
If anyone believes this nonsense, here are the facts he is counting on you not knowing.

The deal did not end Iran's nuclear program. It rented a pause. Iran kept its centrifuges, kept Fordow buried in a mountain, kept enriching to 3.67%, and the key restrictions came with expiration dates. The sunset clauses began lifting in 2025. Obama's own answer at the time was that breakout time "would have shrunk almost down to zero" as the deal expired. His deal scheduled the problem for his successors.

The regime lied its way into the deal. The JCPOA was premised on Iran coming clean about past weapons work. In 2018 Israel pulled Iran's own nuclear archive out of a Tehran warehouse: tens of thousands of documents on the Amad Project, a crash program to build nuclear weapons, preserved and hidden while Iran certified it had no such program. The IAEA later found uranium traces at undeclared sites Iran never explained.

The deal paid for terror. Sanctions relief unfroze roughly $100 billion and the US delivered $1.7 billion in cash. That money flowed to the IRGC, Hezbollah, Hamas, and the Houthis. Diplomacy with a regime at war with you is financing, not peace.

And the result? By 2025 Iran was enriching to 60%, a short technical step from weapons grade, with enough material for multiple bombs and the IAEA declaring it in violation of its obligations. That is what required military force this year. Iran marched to the threshold under the deal's cover and after it.

"I didn't have to fire a missile" is true. He handed the regime money, legitimacy, and a timetable, and left the missiles to be fired a decade later by someone else. Appeasing a dictatorship doesn't buy peace. It buys the dictatorship time.

fordow.tx:
Hidden beneath a mountain, Iran’s Fordow nuclear facility was designed to withstand conventional airstrikes. Then came the GBU-57 Massive Ordnance Penetrator—the US military’s 30,000-pound bunker-buster, engineered to strike deeply buried and heavily fortified targets. 

Dropped by B-2 stealth bombers, the GPS-guided weapon uses its immense weight and hardened casing to penetrate underground before detonating. Its reported penetration capability reaches around 60 metres, while Fordow’s underground facilities are estimated to lie roughly 80–90 metres beneath the mountain.

That raises a critical question: can even America’s most powerful conventional bunker-buster destroy a facility buried deeper than its estimated penetration limit? The answer depends on the structure, geology and effects of the strikes—not just the bomb’s size.

I am the Deputy Director for Continuity of Enrichment at the Atomic Energy Organization of the Islamic Republic of Iran, and I would like to thank the United States Air Force and the Israeli Air Force for performing our annual asset verification.

Last June they dropped bunker-busters on Fordow, Natanz, and Isfahan and announced that the Islamic Republic’s key enrichment facilities had been completely and totally obliterated. I opened the shared drive the next morning. The folder still existed. Someone had renamed it “Temporary Entrance Maintenance—Peaceful Purposes.” The material we had moved the week before was listed under “Off-Site Professional Development.” I approved the rename. It auto-saved. The Supreme Leader’s fatwa against nuclear weapons was already in the folder. It has been in the folder since 2003. It has never been closed.

The fatwa is excellent documentation. It is oral. It is cited. It is never quite published as a classic ruling that would require us to stop. We present it to the IAEA. We present it to visiting ambassadors. We present it to the people who ask why the centrifuges keep turning. The fatwa covers use. The continuity plan covers everything else. Both documents are correct. One of them is temporary. The temporary one is still running.

The Atomic Energy Organization handles the public face: electricity, radiopharmaceuticals, sovereignty, service to humanity. The Organization of Defensive Innovation and Research handles the other face. The IRGC built the tunnels at Fordow because the IRGC builds tunnels. We do not discuss which face is which in the same meeting. We do not need to. The shared drive does not care which letterhead is on the folder.

In February they came back. The first wave hit the compound while the Supreme Leader was still above ground. We marked him “Out of Office—Permanent” and kept the continuity call going. The IRGC commander, the Defense Minister, and several others were marked the same way. The call continued. The new strikes were logged as incomplete because the knowledge had already been restructured around the material that survived the previous incomplete strikes. The restructuring was finished before the second round started. The second round is still listed as “In Progress.” It has been in progress for eight months. The Islamic Republic remains in the header.

Now the Space Force watches everything. They can read a name badge from orbit. We issued guidance that no one is to wear a name badge. The guidance is followed. Last week a technician arrived in a jacket that still had the old badge sewn into the lining. The satellite noted the stitching. We have opened a ticket. The ticket is currently assigned to Facilities. Facilities was struck in June. Facilities has not responded. The jacket is still in the system.

The latest American statement says there isn’t much activity at the remaining sites. Our latest report says the same thing. The two reports match. Matching reports are what we track. Activity is defined as anything that produces a useful image on the next pass. We have reduced useful images. We have not reduced the ability to produce them later. The fatwa is still in the folder. The material is still in the folder. The people who remember how the machines go together are still employed by the Islamic Republic.

I am sometimes asked if the program continues. The program continues in the form it has always continued under the Islamic Republic: residual material that was not destroyed, machines that can still be assembled, and a shared drive that survived two rounds of bunker-busters because no one thought to bomb the shared drive. None of these items require a new hall. All of them require that no one stand still long enough for the next satellite to finish spelling the name on the jacket.

natanz.tx:
Trump says the “Mother of All Bombs” is “like a tiny nuclear bomb.” He’s already blurring the line. Here’s what an actual tiny nuclear bomb does.

The Davy Crockett, the smallest nuke the US ever built, had a yield of about 20 tons of TNT. The MOAB is about 11 tons, so the blast radius is almost the same.

The difference is radiation. Buildings collapse out to about 150 m, but a lethal radiation dose reaches about 380 m. In this Midtown simulation, around 900 people die on day one, about 4,500 more die in the following weeks, and about 2,300 die of cancer over the next 50 years.

Now Trump has his sights on Pickaxe Mountain, Iran’s nuclear site buried up to 100 m in granite near Natanz. “We’ll knock it out fast,” he says.

The problem is that the MOAB likely can’t reach that deep. When conventional bombs can’t finish the job, only one option is left, and analysts like Robert Pape warn Trump could face pressure to use it.

A nuclear bunker-buster wouldn’t stay underground. It burrows only a few meters before it detonates, making it a ground burst, the dirtiest kind. It throws radioactive rock into the sky, which then falls wherever the wind carries it.

In 2010, Bill Ryan of Project Avalon went public with a whistleblower’s account of a planned war. It starts with a strike on Iran that provokes a nuclear response. A brief, “limited” nuclear exchange follows, then a ceasefire.

Sixteen years later, the US and Israel are at war with Iran, and “tactical” nukes are openly debated.

Trump says he “wouldn’t use nuclear.” He also says the bomb he’s considering is “like” one. If the mountain is still standing after the MOAB, watch which word wins.

As Midterms and Israeli elections loom on the horizon, there is a growing feeling that we are currently on the eve of another large-scale military campaign against Iran.

Several indicators are pointing to the resumption of large-scale combat operations by the United States and Israel in Iran in the near future:

1) On October 21, NBC News reported, citing US officials and people familiar with the matter, that the US military has quietly been scaling back its troop presence at bases across the Middle East in recent days, while the State Department has ordered a further reduction in staff at multiple diplomatic posts in the region. One of the sources said that the withdrawal of American forces and diplomatic personnel is similar to drawdowns at bases and embassies that the Pentagon and State Department initiated before the beginning of the war with Iran back in February.

2) Earlier this week, Israeli Air Force conducted a long-range sortie through the Syrian and Iraqi airspace toward Iranian border, consistent with the profile of simulated strike against Iran. The exercise involved dozens of fighter jets and numerous refueling aircraft. According to Axios, some U.S. sources said they had the impression that Israel was hoping the Iranians would fire at the aircraft, providing a justification for launching strikes against Tehran. 

3) In mid-October, Axios also reported that US President Trump and Israeli PM Netanyahu discussed the possibility of launching a major new operation against Iran before the Israeli and U.S. elections, according to two American officials, one Israeli official and a fourth source with knowledge of the matter. An Israeli official said Trump initially seemed to be leaning toward resuming attacks, but then grew more hesitant, but another source said Israeli and U.S. militaries remained on alert and concluding preparations to be ready in case he changes his mind.

4) Anticipating the renewed attack by the US and Israel, Iran has began fortifying its defenses, rallying loyalists and threatening a wider, harsher response against Washington and its Gulf allies, according to WSJ story from mid-October. The outlet also wrote that the Iranians have reinforced protection around its nuclear sites and other security-related bunkers. The efforts included construction of passive defense measures such as makeshift dirt mounds around its Pickaxe Mountain and Natanz nuclear sites to impede any attempted raid by ground forces.

5) On October 19, the Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth made an unannounced visit to Israel, where he met Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at Ovda Air Base. The meeting also included Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz. IDF Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir and other senior Israeli officials were reportedly not invited, for confidentiality reasons. Hegseth arrived via military transport rather than a standard US government aircraft to keep the trip low-profile. 

The new military operation against Iran might involve intense strikes targeting nuclear sites, energy infrastructure, and missile/drone arsenals as a way to force Tehran to accepting terms it has so far resisted after nearly eight months of conflict, sanctions, and the US naval blockade. Iran has refused to move enriched uranium abroad or make nuclear concessions, and it has used leverage over the Strait of Hormuz. 

It's also noting that the Iranian economy suffered severe strain due to US naval blockade of Iranian ports and intensified sanctions. Oil exports have largely collapsed, while the inflation remains extremely high. The renewed bombing campaign against energy and economic targets could be a factor that pushes the Iranian economy "over the brink" and forces the regime to make concessions.

I am the Deputy Director for Continuity of Enrichment at the Atomic Energy Organization of the Islamic Republic of Iran, and I would like to thank the United States Air Force and the Israeli Air Force for performing our annual asset verification.

Last June they dropped bunker-busters on Fordow, Natanz, and Isfahan and announced that the Islamic Republic’s key enrichment facilities had been completely and totally obliterated. I opened the shared drive the next morning. The folder still existed. Someone had renamed it “Temporary Entrance Maintenance—Peaceful Purposes.” The material we had moved the week before was listed under “Off-Site Professional Development.” I approved the rename. It auto-saved. The Supreme Leader’s fatwa against nuclear weapons was already in the folder. It has been in the folder since 2003. It has never been closed.

The fatwa is excellent documentation. It is oral. It is cited. It is never quite published as a classic ruling that would require us to stop. We present it to the IAEA. We present it to visiting ambassadors. We present it to the people who ask why the centrifuges keep turning. The fatwa covers use. The continuity plan covers everything else. Both documents are correct. One of them is temporary. The temporary one is still running.

The Atomic Energy Organization handles the public face: electricity, radiopharmaceuticals, sovereignty, service to humanity. The Organization of Defensive Innovation and Research handles the other face. The IRGC built the tunnels at Fordow because the IRGC builds tunnels. We do not discuss which face is which in the same meeting. We do not need to. The shared drive does not care which letterhead is on the folder.

In February they came back. The first wave hit the compound while the Supreme Leader was still above ground. We marked him “Out of Office—Permanent” and kept the continuity call going. The IRGC commander, the Defense Minister, and several others were marked the same way. The call continued. The new strikes were logged as incomplete because the knowledge had already been restructured around the material that survived the previous incomplete strikes. The restructuring was finished before the second round started. The second round is still listed as “In Progress.” It has been in progress for eight months. The Islamic Republic remains in the header.

Now the Space Force watches everything. They can read a name badge from orbit. We issued guidance that no one is to wear a name badge. The guidance is followed. Last week a technician arrived in a jacket that still had the old badge sewn into the lining. The satellite noted the stitching. We have opened a ticket. The ticket is currently assigned to Facilities. Facilities was struck in June. Facilities has not responded. The jacket is still in the system.

The latest American statement says there isn’t much activity at the remaining sites. Our latest report says the same thing. The two reports match. Matching reports are what we track. Activity is defined as anything that produces a useful image on the next pass. We have reduced useful images. We have not reduced the ability to produce them later. The fatwa is still in the folder. The material is still in the folder. The people who remember how the machines go together are still employed by the Islamic Republic.

I am sometimes asked if the program continues. The program continues in the form it has always continued under the Islamic Republic: residual material that was not destroyed, machines that can still be assembled, and a shared drive that survived two rounds of bunker-busters because no one thought to bomb the shared drive. None of these items require a new hall. All of them require that no one stand still long enough for the next satellite to finish spelling the name on the jacket.

pickaxe.t: The conditions that enabled the first Trump-Iran deal have changed. The new conditions suggest no durable US-Iran deal will emerge until Trump’s term ends. Thi…
pickaxe.tx:
The conditions that enabled the first Trump-Iran deal have changed. The new conditions suggest no durable US-Iran deal will emerge until Trump’s term ends. This has significant implications for Trump's potential use of a MOAB against Pickaxe Mountain.

In February, the Iranians still believed a deal with Trump was possible. They saw Trump as a president who yearned to be historic - either by striking a deal with Tehran or by becoming the president who got rid of the Islamic Republic. If the latter proved impossible, Trump was still attracted to the idea of a deal.

Tehran no longer holds this view. Instead, Trump is seen as an inherently unstable and immature person who may want a deal, but does not have the discipline to secure one or the strength to keep it in the face of attacks from Israel and pro-Israeli forces in the US.

Moreover, the Iranian narrative suggests that Trump did not hurt enough before agreeing to the MOU. Had the war been more costly, he would have had stronger incentives to keep the agreement.

Combined with the idea that he cannot keep a deal, this results in an Iranian perception that the war can only end once the cost of continuing it becomes intolerable for Trump.

That is, incentives or face-saving exits won’t end the war; Trump reaching a military dead-end will.

These perceptions profoundly shape the implications of Trump striking Pickaxe Mountain with a MOAB.

Tehran’s likely reaction will be to expand the war significantly. Iran’s experience with Trump is that he backs off only if Tehran inflicts high costs on his strategy.

A proportional Iranian response to an attack on Iran’s nuclear facilities would be to strike at other nuclear facilities in the region, including in the UAE and Israel. While this would significantly destabilize the region, Tehran believes only such a response would prompt Trump to back off.

hodeidah.tx:
🇾🇪|The Fall of Jabal Han: The Last Barrier West of Taiz Vanishes in Ten Minutes

October 20, 2026. Saudi-backed mobilization forces have withdrawn from Jabal Han.

Jabal Han is no ordinary mountain. It is the highest vantage point west of the city of Taiz. Its artillery positions command the main roads leading into the city's western sector, and its observation posts monitor every vehicle entering or leaving Taiz. Its fortifications, reinforced repeatedly over the last decade, were considered the final, impenetrable barrier west of Taiz.

Yet once Ansarallah completed their encirclement, this barrier could not withstand a single decisive offensive.

💥 The Geometry of Encirclement

The fall of Jabal Han was not the result of a direct frontal assault. Ansarallah did not attempt to storm the mountain slopes from the west. Instead, they bypassed it.

First, they seized Al-Murab'ah and the Al-Ariel heights, severing the link between Jabal Han and its rear supply lines. They then tightened the noose, leaving the defenders on the mountain to realize they were no longer holding a defensive position. They had become besieged hostages.

Faced with a choice, to have their soldiers wiped out one by one in their positions or to retreat, the commanders chose to withdraw.

Jabal Han did not fall because it was stormed. It fell because it was bypassed. And the very force that bypassed it now stands atop its summit.

🎯 The Western Flank Opened

Jabal Han lies to the west of Taiz. To its south is the direction of the old airport. To its east, the city's built-up urban area. And to its north, the highway connecting Taiz to Hodeidah.

All three directions now lie within the line of sight of Ansarallah.

The defensive architecture of the Saudi-backed forces in Taiz relies on a network of mutually supporting key heights. Jabal Han served as the linchpin of that western defense. With the key strongpoint removed, the western defensive line is no longer a continuous front. It has been fractured into a series of isolated, disconnected positions.

The fall of Taiz is not merely imminent. It is already underway. Jabal Han is the penultimate node. The final node lies within the city streets themselves.

📜 Who Turned Taiz into a Battlefield?

Taiz has been under siege for years. It is not Ansar Allah that has besieged the city. Rather, it is those who transformed the city into a military stronghold.

They looted shops in the city center and padded their ranks with ghost soldiers. As Ansar Allah advanced, they retreated, abandoning their positions and fleeing to Aden. They released criminals from prisons, rearmed them, and unleashed them back into the city to terrorize the civilian population. They severed vital supply routes, turned the entire city into a military target, and then demanded that civilians take up arms to defend their homes.

The defenders at Jabal Han have retreated. The civilians trapped in the city have nowhere left to go.

⚔️ Saudi Arabia's Calculus

Saudi Arabia has poured funds, weaponry, training, and command coordination into Taiz. In return, it has received nothing but a string of retreats: the old airport, the Al-Hanjar checkpoint, Jabal Han, and every other strongpoint along the western front.

Saudi Arabia's war budget could purchase equipment, but it could not buy men willing to hold the high ground on its behalf.

The defenders at Jabal Han were not wiped out in battle. They were abandoned, forsaken by their commanders, by their political leadership, and by a government that holds meetings in Aden, signs contracts in Riyadh, and appears on television to claim, look at what we are doing.

Long live the people of Taiz. Long live Yemen. Long live Ansar Allah. Long live the Resistance. Long live the Axis of Resistance.

“The Houthis are here to stay. They’re not going to be defeated, and they’re going to remain in control of a large part of Yemen for the foreseeable future,” former MI6 chief Sir John Sawers said yesterday.

If he was talking about Zaydi Muslims in general, I might have agreed with him. 
Nobody has ever defeated Yemen’s Zaydis - not the Ottomans, not Egypt, not anyone. The northern highlands have swallowed foreign armies for centuries.

But the Houthis are not the Zaydis! They are a modern political-military movement that draws mainly from Zaydi communities in northern Yemen yet does not represent them! Classical Zaydis reject the hidden Imam, do not practice taqiyya the way Iranian Twelvers do, and have historically stood closer to Sunni jurisprudence and theology than to Iran’s system. What the Houthis practice today has far more in common with Iran’s Twelver revolutionary Shiism than with traditional Zaydism!

the Houthi missiles that have hit Riyadh's airport and Aramco's headquarters this month are part of a negotiation over how Yemen comes under Gulf control.

Saudi Arabia and the UAE divided the southern Red Sea between them in January to prepare for it while everyone thought they were going to go to war with each other. 

The UAE left Yemen without leaving the Red Sea. Israel recognized Somaliland across the strait, where the Dubai company DP World owns 65% of the port of Berbera. 

Saudi Arabia now holds the Arabian shore of the Bab el-Mandeb through the Yemeni government it backs, and the UAE holds the ports on the African shore, which is where any Israeli security role in the area would sit, outside Saudi territory. 

Now what the Houthis want was already agreed in principle in December 2023: public salaries paid, Hodeidah port and Sanaa airport reopened, oil exports resumed. 

Iran cannot pay for any of it while the US Navy blockades its own ports, so the Gulf is the only party able to meet that price.

Once Washington and Tehran agree terms for Hormuz, the Houthis reason to keep firing goes with it. 

There's going to be a single Yemeni government.

sanaa-airport.tx:
"The Houthi attacks on our ally Saudi Arabia are absolutely despicable."

Steady on. Despicable is a big word for a Tuesday.

Some context you left out. Saudi has been bombing Yemen since March 2015. Over 150,000 dead in the fighting, tens of thousands of them civilians. Largely with our kit. Typhoons, bombs, missiles. 6,800 BAE Systems staff on the ground keeping the Saudi air force in the air, and £17.6bn of BAE sales since 2015. We are not even in the coalition. We just supply the planes.

And this round did not come from nowhere. On 13 July the Houthis hit Abha airport, after Saudi airstrikes hit Sanaa airport. Their spokesman says they will keep going until the kingdom stops attacking Yemen. That is not despicable. It is a reply.

So one small question. Saudi has one of the largest defence budgets on earth and eleven years of bombing behind it. Why does it need our Typhoons to defend its own airspace from a country it has bombed for eleven years?

"Ally" is a lovely word. In this case it is also an invoice.

suez.t: In October 1943, Germany was losing the war on every front. But at the behest of the Grand Mufti, Luftwaffe intelligence officers were studying how to bomb Tel…
suez.tx:
In October 1943, Germany was losing the war on every front. But at the behest of the Grand Mufti, Luftwaffe intelligence officers were studying how to bomb Tel Aviv.

Their assessment considered the city “the citadel of Palestinian Jewry and émigré Jews.” Unlike Jerusalem, whose population was a little more than half Jewish and which contained Christian and Muslim holy sites, Tel Aviv was nearly 100% Jewish. The Nazis determined that bombing there would kill the maximum number of Jews. Officers noted that the city had no major military installations of value. The point was not strategic advantage, but to kill Jews.

The idea had been pushed by Amin al-Husseini, who was then in Berlin collaborating with the Nazis. He and others had repeatedly asked for attacks on Tel Aviv. Earlier in the summer of 1943, a similar proposal reached Hermann Göring and was rejected because the Luftwaffe no longer had any long-range capacity to spare. Yet the intelligence section still produced a detailed demographic and targeting study.

One officer, First Lieutenant Zetsche, discussed a possible symbolic raid on the Jewish Agency building in Jerusalem around the anniversary of the Balfour Declaration, while acknowledging that Jerusalem itself offered no military importance. The preferred option remained Tel Aviv because it maximized Jewish casualties.

The plan never advanced to an attack since, by late 1943, the Luftwaffe lacked the forces to carry out the raid and Germany’s position in the Mediterranean had collapsed. But the existence of the study shows that, even in retreat, some Nazi planners continued to treat the murder of Jewish civilians in Mandate Palestine as an aspirational objective.

Earlier in the war, an Einsatzgruppe had been prepared to exterminate the Jews of Mandate Palestine in the event of an Axis advance beyond the Suez Canal. When that front failed at the Battle of El Alamein, aerial bombardment was one of the remaining options under discussion.

The fact that the assessment was written by Luftwaffe intelligence officers, not the SS, makes the antisemitic reasoning especially clear: they openly weighed which city would kill the most Jews.

suez.t: October 23, 1942. At twenty minutes to ten at night, in the desert of Egypt, more than eight hundred British guns open fire at once, and the darkness erupts in…
suez.tx:
October 23, 1942. At twenty minutes to ten at night, in the desert of Egypt, more than eight hundred British guns open fire at once, and the darkness erupts into a wall of flame and thunder that can be felt in the chest from miles away. The Second Battle of El Alamein has begun. It is the battle that will finally break Rommel in the desert, the hinge of the whole war in North Africa, and the victory that Churchill would say marked "the end of the beginning."

I have been following the desert war since the early days of this series, Rommel the Desert Fox running the British ragged back and forth across Libya and Egypt, the see-saw campaign that had swung all the way to El Alamein, the last defensible line before the Nile, the Suez Canal, and the oil of the Middle East. In the summer Rommel had been stopped there, barely, in the first battle. Now the British Eighth Army had a new commander, Bernard Montgomery, a careful, methodical, supremely confident general who had rebuilt the army's morale and refused to attack until he had overwhelming strength.

And by October he had it. Montgomery had built up a crushing superiority, in men, in tanks, in guns, in aircraft, in supplies, far more than Rommel could match, because the Axis supply line across the Mediterranean was being strangled while the British were pouring reinforcements, including masses of new American-built Sherman tanks, into Egypt. Rommel himself was away sick in Germany when the blow fell, his army dug in behind vast belts of mines and wire the Germans grimly called the "Devil's Gardens."

Montgomery's plan was not clever maneuver but deliberate, grinding attrition, a battle he called "crumbling." It opened on the night of the 23rd with one of the greatest artillery bombardments since the First World War, those eight hundred-plus guns firing in a stupendous barrage that announced the offensive and smashed at the Axis positions. Then the infantry went in, in the moonlight, to clear paths through the enormous minefields so the armor could pass, and the fighting settled into a brutal, close-quarters slog through the mines and the dug-in defenses.

It was not quick. For days the battle hung in the balance, the British grinding forward yard by yard through the Devil's Gardens, taking heavy losses, the attack at times seeming to stall. Rommel rushed back from Germany to take command, but he had no answer to Montgomery's material superiority and his relentless pressure, and critically he was running out of fuel, his tanks increasingly immobilized for lack of petrol. Montgomery kept up the attrition, wearing the Axis forces down, destroying tanks he could replace and Rommel could not, until at last, in early November, he concentrated his armor and punched through.

Rommel's front broke. Against Hitler's furious orders to stand and die, Rommel, to save what was left of his army, began a long retreat westward across the desert, a withdrawal that would not stop for hundreds of miles. The Axis army in the desert had been decisively beaten for the first time, and it would never recover the initiative. Combined with the Anglo-American landings in northwest Africa that came just days later, El Alamein doomed the entire Axis position in North Africa.

The victory meant an enormous amount, and not just militarily. It was the first great, clear-cut British land victory over the Germans in the whole war, coming after years of defeats and retreats, and it was desperately needed for Allied morale. Church bells were rung in Britain to celebrate. Churchill captured its meaning in one of his famous lines: "Now this is not the end. It is not even the beginning of the end. But it is, perhaps, the end of the beginning." The tide in the west had turned, and it turned here, in the desert, beginning with those eight hundred guns firing into the dark on the night of the 23rd.

suez.t: 70 years ago today, on the 22nd of October 1956, France, Britain and Israel started negotiating a sinister deal at Sèvres. Israel would attack Egypt. France an…
suez.tx:
70 years ago today, on the 22nd of October 1956, France, Britain and Israel started negotiating a sinister deal at Sèvres. Israel would attack Egypt. France and Britain would order both sides to retreat. Nasser would refuse. France and Britain would then a have a casus belli to bomb Egypt. 

On 30 October 1956, Britain and France issued an ultimatum to Egypt and Israel. Stop fighting, withdraw your armies from the Suez Canal, or we will intervene to restore peace.

Sounds ever so benign, right? 

Or ever so cunning. 

They had secretly arranged the war themselves.

A few months earlier, Egyptian president Gamal Abdel Nasser had nationalised the Suez Canal Company, which had been controlled by British and French interests.

The canal was on Egyptian territory, but Britain and France were used to deciding what happened there.

Nasser wanted the canal's revenues to help finance the Aswan High Dam, after the USA and Britain withdrew their offers to help finance its construction.

London was furious. 

Paris was 'pas amusé' either to say the least. French elites had special beef with Nasser over his support for the Algerian struggle against French colonial rule.

Israel had its own reasons to confront Egypt, including Egyptian restrictions on Israeli shipping and violent cross-border conflict.

Three governments with different grievances came together in one of history's most cynical ways. 

On 22 October 1956, senior representatives of Britain, France and Israel gathered secretly at Sèvres, outside Paris.

Among the Israeli participants were Prime Minister David Ben-Gurion, Moshe Dayan and Shimon Peres.

Over the following days they worked out a devious plan.

Israel would invade Egypt's Sinai Peninsula.

Britain and France would then demand that both sides withdraw from the Suez Canal.

Egypt would have to withdraw its forces from part of its own territory and allow foreign troops to occupy strategic positions along the canal.

The planners expected Nasser to refuse.

That refusal would give Britain and France their excuse to attack Egypt.

The agreement was signed on 24 October.

Five days later, Israel invaded.

On 30 October, Britain and France delivered their ultimatum.

The following day, British and French aircraft began bombing Egyptian targets.

Port Said got treated to bombardment, fighting and civilian casualties.

But then the plan ran into obstacles.

American president Dwight Eisenhower refused to support the operation. 

Washington applied enormous diplomatic and financial pressure. 

The Soviet Union threatened intervention.

Britain and France accepted a ceasefire on 6 November.

The invasion became a political humiliation. Nasser remained in power, and Egypt retained control of the canal.

It wasn't bad enough. Officials had to add shameless hypocrisy to the mix. 

On 20 December 1956, British Prime Minister Anthony Eden told the House of Commons that his government had possessed no foreknowledge that Israel would attack Egypt.

Yet British representatives had participated in the negotiations specifying precisely when Israel would attack.

The British diplomat who signed the secret agreement, Patrick Dean, had even returned to Paris the following day in an effort to destroy copies of the document.

Mortifying. 

Israel had to add sickening cruelty to the stinking cocktail. 

On 3 November 1956, during Israel's invasion of Egypt, Israeli troops occupied Khan Yunis in Gaza. There 275 Palestinians were reported killed, according to the UN. 

Palestinian witnesses described the killing of unarmed civilians, while Israel claimed its soldiers had encountered armed resistance.

Abdel Aziz al-Rantisi, 9 at the time, could hear the whole town wailing and wailing. Joe Sacco and Chris Hedges spoke to him decades ago and recently mentioned this haunting detail at a talk about their new book, Requiem for Gaza. 

That's how it goes. Elites hatch neat plans in warm rooms with delicious food, apathetic to who will be squished.

🚨 BREAKING: President Trump announces the Department of War will be investing $1.5 BILLION in semi-conductor chip production in NORTH CAROLINA

This is MASSIVE news.

Right now, the reason the US is forced to defend Taiwan is because they practically control the semi-conductor industry.

Semi-conductors are needed for practically EVERY SINGLE advanced electronic device you use on a daily basis. We cannot have ANY other country controlling semi-conductors. That is absolutely a national security priority.

taiwan-strait.tx:
President Trump just announced the Department of War is investing $1.5 billion into semiconductor chip production right here in North Carolina. This is bigger than a factory headline.
For years the U.S. has been dangerously dependent on Taiwan for the advanced chips that power everything from your phone and car to military radar, drones, missile defense, and the AI systems we now call Super Intelligence. One disruption in the Taiwan Strait and the entire supply chain for modern electronics and national defense is at risk. COVID already showed us how fragile that dependence is.
This investment—tied to domestic production of specialized materials like silicon carbide and gallium nitride—moves critical manufacturing onto American soil. Those materials aren’t ordinary chips; they’re the high-performance components needed for power systems, electronic warfare, and next-generation defense tech. Building them in North Carolina creates real jobs, strengthens the industrial base, and reduces the leverage any foreign power has over our technology and security.
It’s not just about one state. It’s about making sure the devices we use every day and the systems that protect the country are no longer held hostage by geography or geopolitics. American manufacturing, American workers, American control of the technology that runs the 21st century. That’s the actual substance behind the announcement.

taiwan-strait.t: Gideon Rachman asks whether the world is “sleepwalking into World War III?” It’s a long read, and not a terribly enlightening one. Rachman tours Ukraine, the G…
taiwan-strait.tx:
Gideon Rachman asks whether the world is “sleepwalking into World War III?”

It’s a long read, and not a terribly enlightening one. Rachman tours Ukraine, the Gulf, the Taiwan Strait and the 65 conflicts currently raging around the world, and finds the culprits to be “revisionist powers”, “strongman leaders” and an “axis of adversaries”: Russia, China, Iran and North Korea.

In a couple of thousand words, he finds no space at all for the crisis of neoliberal capitalism, albeit he does note the important fact that the G7, which accounted for two-thirds of world output in 1989, is now down to 43 percent.

Lenin would have recognised the connection between this decline and the attempt by declining powers to use military means to hold on to a world they can no longer dominate economically. He would have easily recognised “the striving for domination, not for freedom”.

More than a century after his death, Lenin remains a far better and more relevant guide to the questions of war and peace than the FT’s chief foreign affairs commentator.

Imperialism is hitting out in all directions:

• Genocide in Gaza, armed and financed by Washington, London and Berlin.

• US-Israeli criminal war on Iran and Lebanon.

• A proxy war in Ukraine to weaken and dismember Russia.

• Economic warfare against China: tariffs, chip bans, sanctions, blacklists.

• A “Donroe Doctrine” under which a president is kidnapped, Cuba is placed under a genocidal energy siege, and election results are determined in Washington DC.

• AUKUS, RIMPAC, Talisman Sabre, and a ring of US bases around China’s coast.

None of this features as a cause of insecurity in Rachman’s telling. He’s more worried about whether Xi Jinping “considers that America’s Taiwan Relations Act means something”, or whether Putin sees NATO’s Article Five as an “iconclad commitment”.

In other words, his proposed path to peace is for the US to make its threats more credible. Peace through NATO. Peace through imperialism.

The real guarantee of peace is a multipolar world where no power gets to dictate terms to the rest – exactly what Rachman’s “axis of adversaries” is working towards, and exactly what the West is fighting to prevent.

qt.t:
Two letters purportedly written by Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr to a US official have surfaced online. Both letters name Peter Enzminger as the recipient. He is listed as a counselor at the US Embassy in Manila and is reportedly linked to the CIA.

·The first letter, dated July 31, 2026, says the US interests are the "highest guiding principle" of Teodoro's official duties. It suggests Philippine operations near Ren'ai Reef were deliberately conducted to provoke China, even at risk to Philippine personnel, and presents his possible rise to the presidency as strategically advantageous to the US.

·The second, dated May 29, 2026, but circulated later, discusses pushing a multibillion-dollar purchase of F-16 fighter jets and other US weapons. It suggests major defense purchases were used to win favor with Washington.

The Philippine Department of National Defense has called the first letter fake, while the second remains unverified. But the allegations demand a serious and independent investigation. If proven true, they would suggest Teodoro's actions serve neither Philippine interests nor the country's sovereignty. #MediaUnlocked

Leaked letters purportedly from Philippine Defense Secretary Teodoro to a CIA-linked US Embassy counselor state that US interests are the "highest guiding principle" of his official duties — and that Ren'ai Reef ops were deliberately staged to provoke China, even at risk to Filipino personnel

🇵🇭 Manila is scrambling to call these leaked letters "fake," which is hilarious because even if they were forged, whoever wrote them just copied and pasted current Philippine defense policy. Gen. Clark casually revealed that in America's war planning against China, everyone gets a job:

🇯🇵 Japan acts as the northern anchor, providing airfields and command integration
🇰🇷 South Korea serves as the arsenal and logistics hub, providing the ammo stockpiles
🇵🇭 The Philippines provides the 7,641 islands to act as the forward firing line (and primary missile sponge)

Gen. Clark is very proud of the new Typhon launchers on Philippine soil — mobile Tomahawks that can hit coastal China, alongside footholds pre-positioned just 100 miles from Taiwan Island. He calls it "deterrence"

Replace the word "deterrence" with "provocation" and things start to make a lot of sense 🇵🇭🎯

Let's look at the actual realities on the ground:

Triangular Division of Labor: The FT article points out a very specific operational supply chain and division of labor among U.S. allies 🇯🇵🇰🇷🇵🇭 in American war planning against China in which the Philippines will play a major role

The 1992-to-2026 "Sovereignty Workaround": The US regained its old Subic/Clark basing footprint without resuming the ownership that got it expelled in the 90s. EDCA bases are legally Philippine-owned; the US is merely a "rotational guest." In a war, those bases are legitimate Philippine targets absorbing strikes — while the US retains the option to pack up and leave

Land Power Solving Naval "Tyranny of Distance": Because the US Navy and Air Force face high risks from China's anti-access/area-denial (A2/AD) systems, the US Army is using the Philippines' 7,641 islands to build its own land-based A2/AD nodes to complicate Chinese naval movements

Dual-Flashpoint Monopoly: The Philippines is the only territory capable of simultaneously monitoring and choking off both the Taiwan Strait (via Batanes in the north, 100 miles from Taiwan) and the South China Sea (via Palawan in the south)

Mission Creep Hidden in Plain Sight: The four new EDCA sites added in 2023 were sold to the public over South China Sea tensions (Scarborough, Second Thomas Shoal). Yet deploying NMESIS anti-ship missiles and Typhon/Tomahawk strike capabilities aimed at coastal China is a pure Taiwan-war mission, not a reef-defense mission. Manila peddled one product; Washington installed another

The South Korea Ammo Detail is the Giveaway: Gen. Clark casually revealed that munitions were shipped directly from Korean stockpiles to sustain Philippine live-fire exercises. That's not "training" — that's rehearsing pre-positioned war stocks along the First Island Chain. It’s logistics choreography for an actual war

The Philippines' job is to complicate Chinese defense planning by making itself the densest cluster of aim points in Southeast Asia — that's Teodoro's "US interests are the highest guiding principle" in action.

US Undersecretary of War Elbridge Colby calls Manila a "model ally." What he actually means is that the Philippines is a model missile sponge: 7,641 islands volunteered to absorb Beijing's return salvo in response to US provocations so Guam, Hawaii, and the US homeland don't have to...

taiwan-strait.t: 🇺🇸 TODAY IN AMERICAN HISTORY: THE TRAGIC FINAL MISSION OF THE USS TANG October 24, 1944 — 82 years ago today. The USS Tang (SS-306) was one of America’s most s…
taiwan-strait.tx:
🇺🇸 TODAY IN AMERICAN HISTORY: THE TRAGIC FINAL MISSION OF THE USS TANG

October 24, 1944 — 82 years ago today.

The USS Tang (SS-306) was one of America’s most successful submarines during World War II.

Under the command of Lieutenant Commander Richard H. O’Kane, Tang carried out five combat patrols against Japanese shipping in the Pacific.

During her final patrol, Tang attacked a Japanese convoy in the Taiwan Strait.

But tragedy struck.

ONE OF HER OWN TORPEDOES CIRCLED BACK AND HIT THE SUBMARINE!

Tang sank in approximately 180 feet of water.

Of the 87 American sailors aboard, only nine survived.

Some of the survivors escaped from the submerged submarine using emergency escape equipment, an extraordinary feat under terrifying conditions.

Those who survived were captured by Japanese forces and held as prisoners of war.

Commander O’Kane survived and later received the Medal of Honor.

78 AMERICAN SAILORS NEVER CAME HOME.

Their courage and sacrifice deserve to be remembered.

🇺🇸 Fair winds and following seas, gentlemen. Your sacrifice will never be forgotten.
