ras-laffan.t: 🇶🇦 QatarEnergy has lined up 3 US deals in 2 days. The world’s second-largest LNG exporter is now buying American LNG. Cheniere Energy, Inc.: signed, 4m tonnes…
ras-laffan.tx:
🇶🇦 QatarEnergy has lined up 3 US deals in 2 days.

The world’s second-largest LNG exporter is now buying American LNG.

Cheniere Energy, Inc.: signed, 4m tonnes a year from 2031 to 2054

Venture Global LNG: in advanced talks for at least 3m tonnes a year

Woodside Energy’s Louisiana LNG: in talks for up to 3m tonnes a year over 15–20 years

If all 3 close, that’s about 10m tonnes a year. 

Add Qatar’s 70% of the 18m-tonne Golden Pass plant in Texas ( ExxonMobil).

Why would Qatar buy gas from someone else?

Because this year a single strait cut off its exports.

When Hormuz shut, QatarEnergy declared force majeure and bought 33 spot cargoes of US LNG, mostly from Venture Global, to keep supplying Korea, Taiwan, India and Japan.

In LNG your reputation depends on delivering. 

Qatar’s customers have 20-year contracts with it. 

If it can’t ship from Ras Laffan, it ships from Louisiana.

Then there’s the price.

Many of Qatar’s long-term Asian contracts are linked to crude oil. 

US LNG costs about 115% of Henry Hub plus a liquefaction fee of around $2.50. 

With Henry Hub near $3, that’s about $6 at the plant before shipping.

So Qatar can buy at a Henry Hub price and sell at an oil-linked price.

Qatar doesn’t set the oil price, but every extra dollar on Brent lifts what its oil-linked buyers pay.

Every US cargo Qatar buys is a cargo Europe and Asia can’t. 

The world’s biggest LNG seller is now bidding against its own customers for American supply.

That’s why JKM and TTF sit near $30.

Qatar is buying a second route out and Henry Hub is starting to shape prices in Doha.

ras-laffan.t: QatarEnergy signing long term contracts to purchase U.S. LNG may be what “Gulf states fend for themselves” looks like in practice. If the U.S. is going from gu…
ras-laffan.tx:
QatarEnergy signing long term contracts to purchase U.S. LNG may be what “Gulf states fend for themselves” looks like in practice. 

If the U.S. is going from guaranteeing energy security to selling it, then Qatar paying for U.S. goodwill with LNG deals now instead of hosting U.S. bases makes sense.

The Qataris have traditionally been clear eyed about their situation and made decent deals. From before the British in Ottoman times to 1915 when the British expressly forbid Ibn Saud from attacking Qatar, Kuwait, and the Sheikdoms that would become the UAE. 

When Qatar became a separate country in 1971, Sheik Al Thani became Emir Al Thani and two days later the U.S. recognized the new nation. 

In the 1990s, Qatar discovered offshore natural gas deposits and transitioned from a poor peninsula of pearl divers to having the highest wealth per capita in the world in one generation and hosting F1 races.

Similar to the House of Saud gaining U.S. support by recycling oil profits into U.S. treasuries, and Bahrain through hosting U.S. naval forces after taking over when the British withdrew east of Suez, Qatar built the largest air base in the Middle East, Al Udeid following the first Gulf War at over $1 billion and invited the U.S. 

Qatar security became synonymous with U.S. national security interest. Now the Qataris are shifting strategies by buying U.S. LNG after Ras Laffan took missile hits. 

The contract to buy U.S. LNG is for about 5% of Qatar capacity, and they already own 70% of Golden Pass LNG in Texas, so they are diversifying their long term supply outside chokepoints. 

Would Qatar bother if they thought the world was going back to the way things were? 

They are buying long term LNG contracts that don't start until the next U.S. administration and run through 2054. 

Is Qatar being clear eyed about a shift in U.S. policy and aligning themselves with the U.S.'s new policy of selling energy instead of guaranteeing security?

ras-laffan.tx:
The US shipped 147 bcm of LNG last year, 1/3 more than Qatar.

Number 2 on this list has been hit hard since March.

Qatar exported 111 bcm in 2025, per the Energy Institute. 

Then Iran struck Ras Laffan, and Hormuz closed behind it.

Qatar used to supply about 45% of India’s LNG.
 In September it was about 4%.

The US already supplied 93% of global LNG export growth last year. 
This year it’s carrying the market.

The buyers are China at 91 bcm, Japan at 89 and South Korea at 63. They’re bidding against Europe, whose storage is only 74.5% full.

Japan’s power price just hit a four-year high.

Next year’s list will look very different.

ras-laffan.tx: Qatar’s 23-year deal to buy American LNG from Cheniere Energy runs from 2031 through 2054, far outlasting the three-to-five-year repair window for its war-damaged Ras Laffan export terminals. By committing to lift US gas for over two decades after a US-led war triggered the destruction of its own facilities, Doha is effectively paying a generational security rent, ensuring American energy firms profit off the conflict at Qatar's expense well into the 2050s.

ras-laffan.t: Since the outbreak of the Iran war in February, Tehran has focused primarily on imposing costs on the US and its Arab regional partners, particularly by target…
ras-laffan.tx:
Since the outbreak of the Iran war in February, Tehran has focused primarily on imposing costs on the US and its Arab regional partners, particularly by targeting military bases and critical infrastructure across the Persian Gulf.

Israel has also been targeted, but generally less heavily than during the June 2025 war.

The clearest example came in March, when Israel struck Iran's South Pars gas facilities. Rather than retaliating primarily against Israel, Iran struck Qatar's Ras Laffan gas complex, inflicting major damage.

Tehran's central deterrence equation was with Washington: make attacks on Iranian energy infrastructure costly enough for the US and its regional partners (and the global economy by extension) that Trump would restrain Israel. And indeed, Trump subsequently declared on Truth Social that Israel would not strike South Pars again.

Iran also hit Israel's Bazan refinery in March, but the damage was less severe than in June 2025, when Iranian strikes shut down the facility and disrupted operations for months.

Now, amid signs that major fighting could soon resume, Tehran appears to be signaling a renewed focus on establishing deterrence directly against Israel, warning of far greater costs should it attack Iran again.

The IRGC spokesperson has threatened that attacks on Iranian energy infrastructure would leave Israel facing "scorched earth."

Separately, IRGC-affiliated Saberin News had circulated a claim that Iran has decided to use “hypersonic penetrator warheads” against Israeli nuclear facilities if its own are attacked. This purported decision remains unverified.

Yet the emerging message appears to be that Israel itself, not just US partners across the Persian Gulf, could face heavier costs in another round. Still, Iranian strategic deception cannot be ruled out, with Tehran potentially seeking to draw US attention and air defenses toward one theater while striking elsewhere.

Furthermore, successfully penetrating Israeli defenses and inflicting damage on that scale would be more difficult for Iran than in the Persian Gulf. But Iran demonstrated in June 2025 and in 2024 that it could do so (as well as recent precision strikes in Jordan). 

In any case, for Trump and Netanyahu, another escalation would be another huge gamble, even moreso if Tehran is now prepared to impose greater costs directly on Israel rather than relying primarily on pressure through the Persian Gulf.

ras-laffan.tx:
🚨Qatar, sitting on the world's largest gas field, just signed up to buy big volumes of American #LNG through 2054. Let that sink in.

To paraphrase Ronald Reagan's 1984 campaign ad, It's Morning in America's LNG Industry.

Key points:

• Cheniere signed deals to supply @QatarEnergyLNG with up to 4 million tonnes a year from #SabinePass in Louisiana and Corpus Christi in Texas. Deliveries start in 2031.

• Reuters reports Qatar is also in advanced talks with @Venture_Global for at least 3 million more tonnes a year.

• Why? With #Hormuz largely blocked and Ras Laffan damaged, the world's #2 LNG exporter is buying a hedge on the U.S. Gulf Coast.

• The price gap is enormous. Asian spot LNG hit $29.30/MMBtu last week, while Henry Hub sits around $2.84. That's roughly 10 to 1.

• U.S. LNG feedgas demand topped a record 20 Bcf/d on Oct. 19 as Golden Pass ramps up.

• And the fear that exports would drive up U.S. prices? It was never anything more than a leftwing talking point. Not happening. Storage is 35 Bcf above the five-year average, and Henry Hub is under $3.

The lesson here is simple: when even your competitors sign 20-plus-year contracts for your product, the debate is over. 

American #naturalgas isn't a short-lived "bridge fuel." It's the backbone of global energy security, and the world's buyers are voting with their checkbooks.

There is no #energytransition. There is #energyaddition, and American gas is leading it.

[Full breakdown in today's Energy Additions – Link in the next post.]

qt.t:
The US doing a major military escalation against Iran with just 13 days left until the midterms has massive risks for Trump.

No, this is not related to the economic impact of disrupting oil or anything like that.

There's a much more Carter-esque possibility here.

What the US is talking about is a "short, intense campaign" against Iranian infrastructure & likely nuclear facilities.

On more than one occasion in April, Iranian air defenses shot down manned US aircraft. This was after weeks of intense bombardment of air defenses to the point that they were deemed largely gone.

Ever since July, Iran has rapidly been upgrading & rebuilding its air defenses. They are almost certainly stronger than they were back in April in the midst of the heaviest period of joint US-Israeli bombardment.

While it is possible to shoot down a plane at any point, the most likely time would be when Iranian air defenses are most intact & there are the highest number of targets in the air. In this case, the beginning of a new escalation.

There is a significant, non trivial chance a manned aircraft will be shot down. Again, this isn't some questionable Iranian boast, it happened earlier in the war.

Last

ras-laffan.tx:
The idea that more intense kinetic escalation will lead to a clean, quick outcome where Iran surrenders (before or after the midterms) is foolish.

This has been tried multiple times & each time results in a *more* aggressive Iran that lashes out with less restraint.

Is there extreme pain for the Iranian people & lasting damage to the country?

Yes.

Does it result in the Islamic Republic backing down?

Not at all. They don't care.

And the less they have to lose, the more extreme they get. The reason Iran has restrained from extensive strikes on vital regional infrastructure is because it is worried of mutual assured destruction & its own infrastructure getting hit.

If you're going to hit power plants and dams anyway then that restraint goes away.

With every step, Netanyahu & his sadistic zealots at the FDD have lied to Trump that "just one more step" will lead to the end of Iran problem.

This started with assassinations of individuals, small military campaigns, more extreme sanctions, and eventually a 12 day war & a 7 month war.

Yet neither killing Khamenei nor hitting Fordow made the problem go away. There was always magically more work to be done. And additional, more extreme strikes needed.

In response to these actions Iran went from symbolic, coordinated strikes to shooting medium range ballistic missiles in Israeli cities to eventually the destruction of multiple US bases, actually closing the Strait of Hormuz, and even hitting Ras Laffan gas fields (something with global repercussions).

History shows that:

- Yes Israel & the US will be able to get some tactical achievements
- They will not be able to get a strategic victory and the conflict will continue
- Iran will react with a massive escalation that was previously considered too extreme
- There will not be a quick ending
- The US will eventually try to calm things down because the escalations are getting too uncomfortable and things go into a period of relative calm until the cycle is repeated again.

Typically during the periods of relative calm between escalations the US is able to do more sustained damage through economic pressure & the Iranian response is relatively restrained. But the kinetic escalations always lead to unexpected extreme results.

It's very stupid and very risky & any other US president but Trump would not continue to listen to the insane fanatics pushing him that way for yet another round.

fujairah.t: On the 29th of July, 800 kilometres of the Red Sea went to war. No navy was involved. Nobody fired a shot. 4 men in London moved a line on a chart, and somebod…
fujairah.tx:
On the 29th of July, 800 kilometres of the Red Sea went to war. No navy was involved. Nobody fired a shot. 4 men in London moved a line on a chart, and somebody passed the biscuits.
I was holding the biscuits.

There are a handful of us. We meet in a building in the City that wears its plumbing on the outside, and we decide which of the world's oceans are at war.

I know. I think about it on the Central line, usually somewhere around Bank.

I sit on the Joint War Committee. We are underwriters from Lloyd's and the company market, and we publish a list of Listed Areas: the waters where a ship's ordinary cover stops and a premium for war begins. The men who started this business in Edward Lloyd's coffee house in 1688 did not believe in adjectives, and neither do we.

The building is Richard Rogers's. Lifts, ducts and staircases hang off the outside in stainless steel, so from Lime Street it looks like a refinery that went to Cambridge. I've always thought it the only honest building in the City. Everyone else hides the pipes. Inside, the staff wear navy livery with a flash of red and are called waiters, because 3 centuries ago they poured the coffee. They pour the news now.

In the middle of the Room, under the rostrum, hangs the Lutine Bell. It came off a frigate that went down off the Dutch coast in 1799 with a fortune in gold and silver that Lloyd's had insured, and with 240 people aboard, of whom 1 survived. The market paid for the gold in full and quickly, and that payment made our name. The men were not on the policy. The bell was fished up decades later, and for generations a waiter struck it when news came of an overdue ship: once if she was lost, twice if she'd come home.

During the war, Lord Haw-Haw told Britain the bell was ringing day and night for the convoys. It rang once, for the Bismarck. It is cracked now. The last time it rang for a lost ship was 1979.
Every family has an uncle on the wall. Ours is the slave trade. Our market insured the ships, and in June 2020 Lloyd's apologised for its "shameful" role, which in Lloyd's time is roughly the same afternoon. I mention it because people imagine insurance is neutral. It has never been neutral. It decides which voyages happen.

Here is the whole trick, and it embarrasses people with its simplicity. A ship enters a Listed Area. Her owner tells his insurer. The insurer quotes an additional premium for that one voyage, a percentage of what the hull is worth, good for about a week. The owner pays, or he turns round. Nobody has to sink anything. A number does it.

We don't shout. There is no war room. There is a table, a pot of very bad coffee, and Giles. When a strait has become impossible, Giles reads the reports, takes off his glasses and says "interesting." Everyone at the table knows what interesting means. It means the rate has just tripled. You'd have to have been to the right school to hear the violence in it.

We had competition. On February 28 the Americans and the Israelis struck Iran, and Iran began firing at ships in Hormuz. Before the war, a tanker paid us about 0.25% of her value to pass through. In July the President of the United States published a rate card of his own. Every time Iran fired at a ship, he wrote, America would bomb and destroy "ONE BRIDGE OR POWER PLANT." Capitals in the original.

I admired it enormously. It is a tariff schedule. A man who spent his life in property had priced a strait in infrastructure. The difficulty was that nobody sails on his rate card. Owners do not ring the White House before they leave Fujairah. They ring a broker, the broker rings us, and by summer we were quoting between 3% and 10% of the hull per passage. A $100 million tanker paid $3 million to $10 million for a trip shorter than a bank holiday weekend. Giles said "interesting" 4 times that month.

The President can bomb a bridge. He cannot make a ship sail.

fujairah.tx:
French President Emmanuel Macron has begun a three-day Gulf tour to secure extra oil and diesel supplies for France, as the U.S.-Iran war and disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz push up fuel prices. 

He met Kuwait’s emir on Monday and will continue to the UAE, Bahrain and Qatar, joined by the CEOs of TotalEnergies and Engie. 

The Élysée said the goal is “additional volumes and more supplies for the French people,” which it said would indirectly lower prices. 

France is also pushing for routes that bypass Hormuz, such as the UAE’s pipeline to Fujairah. 

The trip comes after nationwide protests over fuel costs, with diesel in France averaging about €2.36 a liter and Brent crude trading near $108 a barrel.

You're blaming the Aquinos for everything, but the actual timeline tells a different story. Cory Aquino didn't kick the US bases out. The Philippine Senate rejected the bases treaty in 1991 despite her efforts to save it, and US forces left in 1992. China occupied Mischief Reef in 1995 under Ramos, not Aquino.

Aquino's son later took China to international arbitration, and the Philippines won in 2016. Duterte then chose closer ties with Beijing instead of fully leveraging that victory. So how does that make the Aquinos responsible for China's actions? Blaming them for everything while ignoring what happened afterward makes no sense.
